Part B: Wasserstein GAN (weight clipping) and WGAN-GP (gradient penalty)¶

Objective¶

Train two Wasserstein GANs on CIFAR-10 — the original WGAN (Lipschitz constraint enforced by weight clipping) and WGAN-GP (Lipschitz constraint enforced by a gradient penalty) — generate random samples, and compute their FID.

A Wasserstein GAN replaces the JS-divergence of the vanilla GAN by the Earth-Mover distance. By Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality

W(P_r, P_g) = sup_{||f||_L <= 1} E_{x~P_r}[f(x)] - E_{x~P_g}[f(x)],

so the discriminator becomes a critic f (no sigmoid, no log) that must be 1-Lipschitz:

  • WGAN: after every critic update the weights are clipped to [-c, c], c = 0.01.
  • WGAN-GP: the constraint is replaced by the penalty λ · E_x̂ [ (||∇_x̂ f(x̂)||₂ − 1)² ], λ = 10, on random interpolates x̂ = ε x_real + (1 − ε) x_fake.

To isolate the Lipschitz mechanism as the only difference, both models use the same generator, the same critic architecture (without any normalisation layer, which is also required for the per-sample gradient penalty) and the same number of critic steps per generator step (n_critic = 5).

Expectation (written before the run) and observed result¶

Expectation — we expected to see:

  • The critic loss -(E[f(real)] - E[f(fake)]) is an estimate of the (negative) Wasserstein distance. Unlike the loss of a vanilla GAN it should decrease in magnitude as training progresses and track sample quality.
  • WGAN-GP clearly beats WGAN with weight clipping. Clipping forces most weights onto the boundary ±c and limits the capacity of the critic, which gives blurry, low-diversity samples and a high FID; the gradient penalty constrains the function rather than the parameters, so the critic stays expressive, training is stable and the FID is much lower (roughly 40-70 for a plain DCGAN-sized model, against 100 or more for clipping).
  • The mean gradient norm of the WGAN-GP critic on interpolates should be driven towards 1 by the penalty.
  • The FID of both GANs should fall steadily during training, and the final WGAN-GP FID should be well below that of the VAE of Part A-1 (and in the range of the VQ-VAE + PixelCNN of Part A-2).

Observed in the run (Prayogshala, RTX 4090) — see the analysis cell at the end of Part B for the full discussion:

  • Confirmed: the Wasserstein estimate falls steadily for both models (WGAN 5.5 → 0.28, WGAN-GP 16.1 → 1.99) while the FID improves.
  • Confirmed: WGAN-GP clearly beats WGAN: FID 63.2 against 116.2 (46 % lower), within the guessed 40-70 and 100+ ranges. Clipping leaves 45 % of the critic weights on the ±0.01 boundary at the end of training.
  • Confirmed: the WGAN-GP gradient norm on the interpolates is driven towards 1 (1.46 at the start, 1.09 at the end).
  • Partly confirmed: the WGAN-GP FID falls steadily over all 25,000 iterations (and was still falling), but the WGAN FID is noisy and rises twice (iterations 15,000-17,500 and 20,000-22,500).
  • Confirmed, and better than guessed: the final WGAN-GP FID (63.2) is well below the β-VAE (141.8) and also below the VQ-VAE + PixelCNN (80-83), not just in its range.

Load the dataset & Normalize the data¶

CIFAR-10 (60,000 colour images, 32x32x3). Pixel values are normalised to [0, 1] as required. The official split is kept (50,000 train / 10,000 test); the whole dataset is held on the GPU as a tensor, which removes the data-loader overhead from every training loop.

Note on the dataset source. The official download server (https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~kriz/cifar-10-python.tar.gz) ran at ~25 kB/s on our GPU machine, so we fetched the same archive from a Hugging Face mirror (huggingface.co/datasets/MIT-OL-AI-D/cifar-10-python) instead. We checked it was byte-identical to the official file: same size (170,498,071 bytes) and same MD5 c58f30108f718f92721af3b95e74349a, the checksum torchvision itself checks. The dataset, split and preprocessing are unchanged; only the download location differs. A copy is in the repo under data/ (split into two parts under 100 MB; see ENV_SETUP.md).

In [4]:
# Load CIFAR-10 and normalise to [0, 1]
def load_cifar10(root="./data"):
    train = torchvision.datasets.CIFAR10(root=root, train=True, download=True)
    test = torchvision.datasets.CIFAR10(root=root, train=False, download=True)

    def to_tensor(arr):
        x = torch.from_numpy(arr).float() / 255.0          # normalise pixels to [0, 1]
        return x.permute(0, 3, 1, 2).contiguous()          # NHWC -> NCHW

    return to_tensor(train.data), to_tensor(test.data)

X_train, X_test = load_cifar10()
X_train = X_train[:N_TRAIN].to(DEVICE)
X_test = X_test.to(DEVICE)

print("train :", tuple(X_train.shape), "range [%.1f, %.1f]" % (X_train.min().item(), X_train.max().item()))
print("test  :", tuple(X_test.shape))
DATA_VAR = X_train.var().item()
print("pixel variance of the training set: %.4f" % DATA_VAR)

Helper Functions¶

Shared utilities: batching, PSNR, parameter counts and image-grid plotting/saving.

In [5]:
def batches(X, batch_size, shuffle=True):
    # yields mini-batches of a GPU tensor
    idx = torch.randperm(len(X), device=X.device) if shuffle else torch.arange(len(X), device=X.device)
    for i in range(0, len(X) - (batch_size - 1 if shuffle else 0), batch_size):
        yield X[idx[i:i + batch_size]]


def psnr_per_image(x, x_hat):
    # PSNR (dB) of every image for data in [0, 1]:  10 log10( 1 / MSE )
    mse = ((x - x_hat) ** 2).flatten(1).mean(1).clamp_min(1e-10)
    return 10 * torch.log10(1.0 / mse)


def count_params(model):
    return sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())


def to_grid(imgs, nrow=10, scale=1):
    # imgs: N x 3 x H x W tensor in [0, 1]  ->  H' x W' x 3 numpy array
    g = torchvision.utils.make_grid(imgs.detach().cpu().clamp(0, 1), nrow=nrow, padding=1, pad_value=1.0)
    g = g.permute(1, 2, 0).numpy()
    if scale > 1:
        g = np.kron(g, np.ones((scale, scale, 1)))
    return g


def show_grid(imgs, title="", nrow=10, scale=1, figsize=(7, 7), save=None):
    g = to_grid(imgs, nrow, scale)
    plt.figure(figsize=figsize)
    plt.imshow(g)
    plt.title(title)
    plt.axis("off")
    plt.tight_layout()
    if save:
        plt.savefig(f"{RES_DIR}/figures/{save}.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.show()


def save_100(imgs, name):
    # keep the 100 images used for the Part-C visual comparison (uint8 -> small files)
    arr = (imgs[:100].detach().cpu().clamp(0, 1).numpy() * 255).round().astype(np.uint8)
    np.save(f"{RES_DIR}/samples/{name}_100.npy", arr)


def update_results(path, key, value):
    # merge one entry into a results JSON file
    data = json.load(open(path)) if os.path.exists(path) else {}
    data[key] = value
    json.dump(data, open(path, "w"), indent=1)

Evaluation metrics: FID, Precision and Recall¶

FID (Frechet Inception Distance) compares the Gaussian statistics (mu, Sigma) of Inception-v3 pool3 features of real and generated images: FID = ||mu_r - mu_g||^2 + Tr(S_r + S_g - 2 (S_r S_g)^(1/2)). Lower is better.

  • Reference statistics: the CIFAR-10 training set.
  • Generated set: N_FID = 10,000 images; every FID in this notebook is the mean +- std of FID_REPEATS independent sampling rounds, so a table entry also shows how noisy the metric is.
  • Inception weights: the standard TF-FID port shipped with pytorch-fid, so the numbers are comparable with published CIFAR-10 FIDs.

As an extra we also report the k-NN Precision / Recall of Kynkaanniemi et al. (2019) on the same features: precision = fraction of generated images that fall inside the real manifold (fidelity), recall = fraction of real images covered by the generated manifold (diversity). FID alone cannot tell "blurry but diverse" apart from "sharp but mode-collapsed"; these two numbers can.

In [6]:
from pytorch_fid.inception import InceptionV3
from pytorch_fid.fid_score import calculate_frechet_distance

inception = InceptionV3([InceptionV3.BLOCK_INDEX_BY_DIM[2048]]).to(DEVICE).eval()


@torch.no_grad()
def inception_features(x, batch_size=250):
    # x: N x 3 x H x W in [0, 1]  ->  N x 2048 float64 numpy features
    out = []
    for i in range(0, len(x), batch_size):
        f = inception(x[i:i + batch_size].to(DEVICE).float())[0]
        out.append(f.squeeze(-1).squeeze(-1).double().cpu())
    return torch.cat(out).numpy()


def gaussian_stats(feats):
    return feats.mean(0), np.cov(feats, rowvar=False)


def fid_from_feats(feats, ref_stats):
    mu, sigma = gaussian_stats(feats)
    return float(calculate_frechet_distance(mu, sigma, ref_stats[0], ref_stats[1]))


# ---- reference statistics (cached on disk) --------------------------------------------------
_ref_path = f"{RES_DIR}/cifar10_inception_ref.npz"
if os.path.exists(_ref_path):
    _z = np.load(_ref_path)
    REF_STATS, REAL_FEATS = (_z["mu"], _z["sigma"]), _z["real_feats"]
else:
    _train_feats = inception_features(X_train)
    REF_STATS = gaussian_stats(_train_feats)
    REAL_FEATS = inception_features(X_test)[:N_FID]            # real manifold for precision/recall
    np.savez(_ref_path, mu=REF_STATS[0], sigma=REF_STATS[1], real_feats=REAL_FEATS)

print("reference stats ready | real features for P/R:", REAL_FEATS.shape)
print("sanity: FID(test set vs train stats) = %.2f   (a perfect generator would sit near this value)"
      % fid_from_feats(inception_features(X_test), REF_STATS))


# ---- precision / recall -----------------------------------------------------------------------
def _kth_radius(X, k=3, bs=1000):
    r = []
    for i in range(0, len(X), bs):
        r.append(torch.cdist(X[i:i + bs], X).kthvalue(k + 1, dim=1).values)   # +1: the point itself
    return torch.cat(r)


def _covered(A, B, rB, bs=1000):
    hit = []
    for i in range(0, len(A), bs):
        hit.append((torch.cdist(A[i:i + bs], B) <= rB[None, :]).any(1))
    return torch.cat(hit).float().mean().item()


@torch.no_grad()
def precision_recall(fake_feats, real_feats=REAL_FEATS, k=3):
    R = torch.from_numpy(real_feats).float().to(DEVICE)
    G = torch.from_numpy(fake_feats).float().to(DEVICE)
    n = min(len(R), len(G))
    R, G = R[:n], G[:n]
    precision = _covered(G, R, _kth_radius(R, k))
    recall = _covered(R, G, _kth_radius(G, k))
    return precision, recall


def evaluate_generator(sample_fn, n=None, repeats=None):
    # sample_fn(n) must return an n x 3 x 32 x 32 tensor in [0, 1].
    # Returns FID mean/std over `repeats` rounds and P/R of the first round.
    n = n or N_FID
    repeats = repeats or FID_REPEATS
    fids, pr, first = [], None, None
    for r in range(repeats):
        set_seed(SEED + 1000 + r)
        imgs = sample_fn(n)
        feats = inception_features(imgs)
        fids.append(fid_from_feats(feats, REF_STATS))
        if r == 0:
            pr = precision_recall(feats)
            first = imgs[:100].detach().cpu()
    return {"FID": float(np.mean(fids)), "FID_std": float(np.std(fids)),
            "Precision": pr[0], "Recall": pr[1]}, first

reference stats ready | real features for P/R: (10000, 2048)
sanity: FID(test set vs train stats) = 3.15   (a perfect generator would sit near this value)

Architectures¶

  • Generator (z ∈ R^128 → 32x32x3): linear → 4x4x256, then three stride-2 transposed convolutions (256→128→64→3) with BatchNorm + ReLU, and a tanh output in [-1, 1].
  • Critic (32x32x3 → R): three stride-2 4x4 convolutions (3→64→128→256) with LeakyReLU(0.2), then a linear layer to a single unbounded score (no sigmoid). No BatchNorm / LayerNorm anywhere in the critic.

The data are scaled from [0, 1] to [-1, 1] for training (matching the tanh generator output) and mapped back to [0, 1] for every metric and picture.

In [7]:
class Generator(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, latent_dim=128):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(latent_dim, 4 * 4 * 256), nn.BatchNorm1d(4 * 4 * 256), nn.ReLU())
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.ConvTranspose2d(256, 128, 4, 2, 1), nn.BatchNorm2d(128), nn.ReLU(),   # 8x8
            nn.ConvTranspose2d(128, 64, 4, 2, 1), nn.BatchNorm2d(64), nn.ReLU(),     # 16x16
            nn.ConvTranspose2d(64, 3, 4, 2, 1), nn.Tanh(),                          # 32x32
        )
        self.latent_dim = latent_dim

    def forward(self, z):
        return self.net(self.fc(z).view(-1, 256, 4, 4))


class Critic(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(3, 64, 4, 2, 1), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2),       # 16x16
            nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 4, 2, 1), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2),     # 8x8
            nn.Conv2d(128, 256, 4, 2, 1), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2),    # 4x4
            nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(256 * 16, 1),
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x).view(-1)


print("generator parameters:", count_params(Generator(CFG["latent_dim"])))
print("critic parameters   :", count_params(Critic()))

generator parameters: 1195587
critic parameters   : 662977

Training and evaluation helpers¶

  • gradient_penalty implements E[(||∇_x̂ f(x̂)||₂ − 1)²] with create_graph=True so that the penalty itself can be differentiated with respect to the critic weights.
  • train_gan(mode, ...) runs the alternating optimisation. In each iteration the critic is trained for n_critic = 5 steps and the generator for one. Optimisers follow the original papers: WGAN uses RMSprop with lr = 5e-5 (momentum-based optimisers were reported to be unstable with clipping); WGAN-GP uses Adam with lr = 1e-4, β = (0.5, 0.9).
  • The logged Wasserstein estimate is E[f(real)] − E[f(fake)]; for WGAN-GP we also log the mean critic-gradient norm on the interpolates, for WGAN the fraction of critic weights that sit on the clipping boundary.
  • An FID checkpoint (with quick_fid_n images, so slightly pessimistic compared with the final 10,000-image FID) is taken every eval_every generator iterations to obtain the FID-versus-iteration curve.
In [8]:
def gradient_penalty(critic, real, fake):
    eps = torch.rand(real.size(0), 1, 1, 1, device=DEVICE)
    x_hat = (eps * real + (1 - eps) * fake).requires_grad_(True)
    grads = torch.autograd.grad(critic(x_hat).sum(), x_hat, create_graph=True)[0]
    norms = grads.flatten(1).norm(2, dim=1)
    return ((norms - 1) ** 2).mean(), norms.mean().item()


@torch.no_grad()
def sample_gan(G, n, bs=1000):
    G.eval()
    out = []
    for i in range(0, n, bs):
        z = torch.randn(min(bs, n - i), G.latent_dim, device=DEVICE)
        out.append((G(z) + 1) / 2)                      # [-1, 1] -> [0, 1]
    G.train()
    return torch.cat(out).clamp(0, 1)


def clip_saturation(critic, c):
    w = torch.cat([p.detach().flatten() for p in critic.parameters()])
    return (w.abs() >= 0.999 * c).float().mean().item()


def train_gan(mode, g_iters, seed=SEED):
    assert mode in ("wgan", "wgan_gp")
    set_seed(seed)
    G, D = Generator(CFG["latent_dim"]).to(DEVICE), Critic().to(DEVICE)
    if mode == "wgan":
        opt_d = torch.optim.RMSprop(D.parameters(), lr=5e-5)
        opt_g = torch.optim.RMSprop(G.parameters(), lr=5e-5)
    else:
        opt_d = torch.optim.Adam(D.parameters(), lr=1e-4, betas=(0.5, 0.9))
        opt_g = torch.optim.Adam(G.parameters(), lr=1e-4, betas=(0.5, 0.9))

    B, zdim, n = CFG["batch_size"], CFG["latent_dim"], len(X_train)
    hist = {"iter": [], "w_dist": [], "critic_loss": [], "gen_loss": [], "grad_norm": [], "clip_frac": [],
            "fid_iter": [], "fid": [], "time": []}
    acc = {"w": [], "d": [], "g": [], "gn": []}
    t0 = time.time()
    for it in range(1, g_iters + 1):
        # ---- critic: n_critic steps --------------------------------------------------------------
        for _ in range(CFG["n_critic"]):
            real = X_train[torch.randint(n, (B,), device=DEVICE)] * 2 - 1
            with torch.no_grad():
                fake = G(torch.randn(B, zdim, device=DEVICE))
            d_real, d_fake = D(real).mean(), D(fake).mean()
            loss_d = d_fake - d_real
            if mode == "wgan_gp":
                gp, gn = gradient_penalty(D, real, fake)
                loss_d = loss_d + CFG["gp_lambda"] * gp
                acc["gn"].append(gn)
            opt_d.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
            loss_d.backward()
            opt_d.step()
            if mode == "wgan":
                for p in D.parameters():
                    p.data.clamp_(-CFG["clip"], CFG["clip"])        # weight clipping
            acc["w"].append((d_real - d_fake).item()); acc["d"].append(loss_d.item())
        # ---- generator: 1 step ---------------------------------------------------------------------
        loss_g = -D(G(torch.randn(B, zdim, device=DEVICE))).mean()
        opt_g.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        loss_g.backward()
        opt_g.step()
        acc["g"].append(loss_g.item())

        if it % CFG["log_every"] == 0:
            hist["iter"].append(it)
            hist["w_dist"].append(float(np.mean(acc["w"]))); hist["critic_loss"].append(float(np.mean(acc["d"])))
            hist["gen_loss"].append(float(np.mean(acc["g"])))
            hist["grad_norm"].append(float(np.mean(acc["gn"])) if acc["gn"] else float("nan"))
            hist["clip_frac"].append(clip_saturation(D, CFG["clip"]) if mode == "wgan" else float("nan"))
            hist["time"].append(time.time() - t0)
            acc = {"w": [], "d": [], "g": [], "gn": []}
        if it % CFG["eval_every"] == 0 or it == g_iters:
            torch.cuda.synchronize()
            t_eval = time.time()
            f = fid_from_feats(inception_features(sample_gan(G, CFG["quick_fid_n"])), REF_STATS)
            hist["fid_iter"].append(it); hist["fid"].append(f)
            t0 += time.time() - t_eval                             # do not count evaluation time as training time
            print(f"{mode:>7} | iter {it:>6}/{g_iters} | W-dist estimate {hist['w_dist'][-1]:8.4f} | "
                  f"grad-norm {hist['grad_norm'][-1]:6.3f} | FID({CFG['quick_fid_n']}) {f:7.2f} | "
                  f"{time.time() - t0:6.0f} s")
    return G, D, hist, time.time() - t0

Extra: latent-space interpolation¶

A generator that has learnt a smooth image manifold (and has not simply memorised the training set) produces gradual, coherent transitions between two random latent codes.

In [14]:
@torch.no_grad()
def gan_interpolate(G, z1, z2, steps=10):
    G.eval()
    a = torch.linspace(0, 1, steps, device=DEVICE)[:, None]
    out = (G((1 - a) * z1 + a * z2) + 1) / 2
    G.train()
    return out

set_seed(11)
zs = torch.randn(8, CFG["latent_dim"], device=DEVICE)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 2, figsize=(15, 6.2))
for c, (name, G) in enumerate([("WGAN", G_wgan), ("WGAN-GP", G_gp)]):
    for r in range(4):
        axes[r, c].imshow(to_grid(gan_interpolate(G, zs[2 * r], zs[2 * r + 1]), nrow=10)); axes[r, c].axis("off")
        if r == 0:
            axes[r, c].set_title(name)
plt.suptitle("Latent interpolation between random noise vectors")
plt.tight_layout()

plt.show()

Analysis: WGAN vs WGAN-GP¶

Both models use the same generator, the same critic architecture (no normalisation), n_critic = 5, batch size 64, and 25,000 generator iterations; the way the Lipschitz constraint is enforced is the only difference (weight clipping, RMSprop vs. gradient penalty, Adam).

Model FID (10k samples) Best FID during training (5k samples) Precision Recall Train time s / generator iter
WGAN 116.2 ± 0.3 117.9 0.629 0.007 12.0 min 0.029
WGAN-GP 63.2 ± 0.3 65.1 0.571 0.152 21.1 min 0.051

(The in-training FIDs use only 5,000 samples and are therefore biased upwards by about 2 points compared with the final 10,000-sample FID.)

(i) Sample quality: WGAN-GP is clearly better¶

WGAN-GP's FID is 53 points (46 %) lower than that of WGAN, a difference more than a hundred times the sampling noise (± 0.3). The FID-versus-iteration curves are separated at every checkpoint (e.g. 168 vs. 230 after 2,500 iterations and 65 vs. 118 at the end). WGAN-GP's curve is smooth and still falling at iteration 25,000, so it has not converged; WGAN's curve flattens and is visibly noisy (it goes up twice: from 123 to 131 between iterations 15,000 and 17,500, and from 118 to 125 between 20,000 and 22,500).

The pictures agree. WGAN produces smeared, washed-out colour patches with a plausible sky/ground layout but almost no object structure. WGAN-GP's samples have recognisable vehicles, animals and scenes with consistent shading and sharper edges, although many are still distorted, as expected from a small DCGAN-size model trained for 25k iterations. In the latent interpolations both generators change smoothly (no jumps, so neither memorises the training set), but the WGAN-GP intermediates keep a coherent object throughout, while the WGAN ones look like drifting colour fields.

(ii) Why: the way the Lipschitz constraint is enforced¶
  • Weight clipping starves the critic. At the end 45 % of WGAN's critic weights sit exactly on the boundary ±0.01, and the figure shows that the fraction stayed between about 36 % and 80 % during the whole run (peaking at about 80 % at 5,000 iterations and staying above 70 % for most of 5,000-12,000). The weights are pushed into a binary-like distribution (two spikes at ±c), so the critic uses only a fraction of its capacity and delivers poor gradients to the generator. The Wasserstein estimate of WGAN is therefore very small (0.28 at the end), because the clipped critic can only realise a loose lower bound of the true distance.
  • The gradient penalty constrains the function, not the parameters. The critic gradient norm on the interpolates falls from about 1.46 at the start to 1.09 at the end, i.e. close to the target of 1 (the penalty is soft and two-sided, so a small residual above 1 is expected), while its weights remain unconstrained — a considerable fraction lies far outside the ±0.01 box (see the weight histogram). The critic stays expressive, and its Wasserstein estimate (1.99) is about seven times larger than that of WGAN.
  • The Wasserstein estimates of the two models are not comparable in absolute value (they are measured with different Lipschitz constraints); what matters is that each falls steadily while sample quality improves, which is the property that makes the WGAN loss useful as a training monitor, unlike the loss of a vanilla GAN. The generator loss of WGAN-GP shows an initial transient (it falls to about -30 in the first 1,500 iterations and then recovers) before it settles, like that of WGAN, in a small range near zero (the absolute level of a generator loss is arbitrary, since the critic output has no fixed offset).
(iii) Precision and recall: read with care¶

WGAN-GP has the much higher recall (0.152 vs. 0.007), i.e. it covers a far larger part of the real-image manifold; WGAN's recall is practically zero, which says that its samples occupy only a narrow region and are far less diverse. WGAN's precision (0.63) is nevertheless higher than that of WGAN-GP (0.57), which contradicts the visual impression and the FID. This is a known weakness of the k-NN precision estimate: when the generated set is concentrated in a dense region of the real feature space, most of its points fall inside real k-NN balls even if the images look poor. We therefore base the quality ranking on FID, recall and the pictures, and do not interpret the precision of WGAN as better fidelity.

(iv) Cost¶

WGAN-GP needs one additional (double) back-propagation per critic step, so an iteration takes 1.75x as long (0.051 s vs. 0.029 s on our RTX 4090), which gives 21.1 vs. 12.0 minutes for the 25k iterations. This is a modest price for a 46 % lower FID. Sampling uses the identical generator, so the sampling times in the table (about 12 ms per 1,000 images for both) only differ by measurement noise.

Summary: both models behave as the WGAN literature describes: the loss is a meaningful training signal, WGAN-GP is more stable, much more diverse and gives a far lower FID than weight clipping at an extra cost of about 75 % per iteration, and the improvement comes entirely from the less restrictive way of enforcing 1-Lipschitzness. In terms of FID the final ranking over all of Part A and Part B is WGAN-GP (63.2) < VQ-VAE + PixelCNN (80-83) < WGAN (116.2) < β-VAE (141.8 for β = 1); Part C discusses this in detail.
